content: This medication is indicated for the induction of remission in patients with active mild-to-moderate distal ulcerative colitis, extending up to 40 cm from the anal verge. The recommended dosage is one metered dose (2 mg) administered rectally twice daily for two weeks, followed by one metered dose rectally once daily in the evening for four weeks. This medication is for rectal administration only and is not intended for oral use. Before administration, patients should empty their bowels. Each applicator is pre-coated with a lubricant; if additional lubrication is required, petrolatum or petroleum jelly may be used. The canister should be warmed in the hands and shaken vigorously for 10-15 seconds before use. The medication can be administered in standing, lying, or sitting positions (e.g., while using the toilet). When applied in the evening, it should be used immediately before bedtime, and patients should avoid emptying their bowels again until the following morning. The safety and efficacy of this medication have not been fully established. There are no results available regarding interactions between budesonide rectal foam and macimorelin. Drugs that directly affect the pituitary secretion of growth hormone (GH) may interfere with the accuracy of the macimorelin diagnostic test. Sufficient washout time of drugs affecting GH release should be allowed before administering macimorelin. Serious interactions may occur between budesonide rectal foam and macimorelin, with an unspecified interaction mechanism. It is recommended to avoid or use an alternative drug. Prolonged use or high doses of corticosteroids, including budesonide, may lead to hypercorticism and adrenal suppression. When transitioning from systemic corticosteroids with higher systemic effects to those with lower effects (e.g., budesonide rectal foam), systemic corticosteroids should be tapered slowly to avoid withdrawal symptoms, including acute adrenal suppression or benign intracranial hypertension. Corticosteroids are known to be immunosuppressive. Patients with active or quiescent tuberculosis, ocular herpes simplex, or untreated fungal, bacterial, systemic viral, or parasitic infections should be monitored closely. Additionally, patients with conditions such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, glaucoma, or cataracts, or those with a family history of diabetes or glaucoma, should be monitored for potential adverse effects of glucocorticosteroids. Patients with moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment should be monitored for increased signs and symptoms of hypercorticism. The use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, indinavir, saquinavir, erythromycin, or grapefruit juice) should be avoided during the six-week treatment period, as these may increase systemic exposure to budesonide. The rectal foam is flammable and should be stored away from flames or heat sources. During pregnancy, this medication is classified as Category C, indicating that risk to the fetus cannot be ruled out. For lactating mothers, budesonide delivered via rectal foam is likely to be present in human milk at low concentrations, similar to budesonide delivered by inhalation from a dry-powder inhaler. Excretion of the drug occurs through urine and feces in the form of metabolites. When adding plans for formulary comparison, users can compare the formulary status of this drug to others in the same class. Formulary information may vary and change over time, so it is recommended to contact the applicable plan provider for the most current information.
